scene_001.title: The First Last Day
scene_001.narration: You are a woman named Diane who is addicted to crack cocaine. You have enough money for two days' rent in the day motel that you currently reside in after working your last client. Then, you receive a call you've come to expect from your patient broker. What do you do?

resource_link.description: Patient brokers are paid to look for addicts or recovering addicts with good insurance that they can then recruit into treatment centers or sober homes.

choices.label: Wait for it to go to voice mail.

resource_link.description: Patient brokers are paid to look for addicts or recovering addicts with good insurance that they can then recruit into treatment centers or sober homes.

scene_002a.title: The Phonecall
scene_002a.narration: You pick up the phone and your patient broker, addressing you by name, explains that he has $3,000 dollars for you if you agree to stay in a sober home for eight days after testing positive for substance use on your insurance.

choices.label: He always pays what he says he will; anything is better than the work I have to do to stay where I am right now. He says my insurance will cover it? I accept this offer.

resource_link.description: Patient brokers work between those with good insurance–their “client,” and the rehab facility, sober home, and/or detox center in exchange for a portion of the insurance money; a part of which is used to entice “clients” into the homes in the first place.

choices.label: Decline the offer. I can find my own help.

resource_link.description: Patient brokers work between those with good insurance–their “client,” and the rehab facility, sober home, and/or detox center in exchange for a portion of the insurance money; a part of which is used to entice “clients” into the homes in the first place.

choices.label: I don't need help. I'm going to find a fix.

scene_002b.title: The Text Message
scene_002b.narration: Your patient broker sends you a text which explains that he has $3,000 dollars for you if you agree to stay in a sober home for eight days after testing positive for substance use on your insurance.

choices.label: He always pays what he says he will, and there's definitely still substance in my system. I accept this offer.

choices.label: Decline the offer. I can find help on my own.

scene_003a.title: In the System
scene_003a.narration: After three days, your insurance has covered your illegal substance test, and your stay at the sober home and so it's time to move in!

choices.label: I'll do my best to stay in the sober home, and stick to the program. I want to recover!

resource_link.description: Sticking to the program is a wise decision. If you got caught with substance, then you could lose out on the $3,000 offered to you by your insurance broker. Although, the rules are inconsistent, manipulative, and sometimes deliberately set up so that the addict will relapse.

choices.label: This sober home is pretty comfortable, so I think I'll stay. Although, one of my housemates says that he got his hands on something good. I think I'll try it with him. Nobody should notice.

resource_link.description: If you got caught with substance, then you could lose out on the $3,000 offered to you by your insurance broker. Although, the rules are inconsistent, manipulative, and sometimes deliberately set up so that the addict will relapse.

choices.label: I can’t take it anymore! I have to get out of here!

resource_link.description: This decision, it seems, is up to you. Sober homes can't keep you against your will (especially without a court order), but failing to stay for the eight days means that you're very unlikely to get your $3,000. Although, the rules are inconsistent, manipulative, and sometimes deliberately set up so that the addict will relapse. Maybe getting out of the cycle: contact a broker, detox, get paid, and relapse isn't such a bad idea..

scene_003b.title: Can one really help themself?
scene_003b.narration: You're tired of being used by people who really don't care about you. You want real help.

choices.label: I've heard good things about the Salvation Army Adult Rehabilitation Centers (ARCs). I think I'll give them a call while my head is still on straight!

resource_link.description: ARCs are free, Christian based, non-profit, requires no insurance, and accepts anyone in any walk of life..

choices.label: Maybe I can do this rehab thing… soon. Just one more fix... it's been so long since my last one.

scene_002c.title: Choosing the Familiar Pain
scene_002c.narration: It’s a strange world, but you've grown familiar with enough of it to find what you're looking for. When you're in too deep, even the surface feels like a rumor

resource_link.description: The first step to solving a problem is admitting that you have it. People are much more likely to stay sober if they have or seek support from people in their lives.

scene_003d.title: Crossing the Rubicon
scene_003d.narration: You wake up after a three day bender. You’re cold, you’re not quite sure where you are, your body aches, and the depression is beginning to set in. It’s now or never–take the rehab or play with fire until the flames play back.

resource_link.description: One estimate is that 3 out of 4 people with a substance use disorder (SUD) will ultimately overcome them despite having fallen off the wagon on occasion.
PYou know where the road leads; you just kept walking.

scene_005a.title: The Help You Needed
scene_005a.narration: Here you are, at the door of a facility that has your best interests and can finally deliver to you the help you need. This is one of the most important decisions that you will ever make, but you have to want… no… you have to need it. Which do you choose?

choices.label: I need it; this is my choice.
I'm sorry, it hurts too much.

scene_win.title: The Help You Needed
scene_win.narration: You choose recovery and accept the support available to you.

scene_relapse.title: Familiar Pain
scene_relapse.narration: One more time becomes another setback, but a setback does not erase the possibility of recovery.
